More volume and variety — if recovery can keep up

5-Day Workout Split: PPL Hybrid, Body-Part or Upper/Lower

Short answer: A push/pull/legs + upper/lower hybrid is the most balanced 5-day split: most muscles get hit twice a week while you keep two rest days.

How a 5-day workout split works

Five days gives you room for higher weekly volume and more exercise variety, which can help intermediate and advanced lifters keep progressing. The trade-off is that recovery and scheduling now matter.

No 5-day structure divides the week perfectly, because five does not split evenly into upper/lower or push/pull/legs. The options below handle that in different ways, and the best one depends on whether you value frequency or focus.

Best 5-day split structures

PPL + Upper/Lower hybrid — PPLUL (recommended)

MonPush
TuePull
WedLegs
ThuRest
FriUpper
SatLower
SunRest

Best for: Intermediates who want most muscles twice a week without a six-day commitment.

Trade-off: Frequency is uneven — push/pull muscles get more weekly hits than legs depending on how you balance upper and lower days.

Classic body-part split

MonChest
TueBack
WedShoulders
ThuArms
FriLegs
SatRest
SunRest

Best for: Lifters who enjoy high volume on one muscle per day and train near-failure on isolation work.

Trade-off: One hit per muscle per week, and a missed session means a missed muscle.

Upper/Lower + weak-point day

MonUpper
TueLower
WedRest
ThuUpper
FriLower
SatWeak points
SunRest

Best for: Four-day upper/lower lifters who want an extra day for lagging muscles.

Trade-off: The fifth day adds volume but also fatigue — keep it short and focused.

Is a 5-day split right for you?

Beginner friendlyLow — more than most beginners need
Muscle buildingExcellent for intermediates
StrengthGood — depends on structure
Schedule flexibilityLow–moderate
Recovery demandHigh
Session length45–70 min
Weekly frequency per muscle1–2× depending on structure

Pros

  • More weekly volume and exercise variety
  • Shorter sessions than 3–4 day plans
  • Easy to add weak-point work
  • Multiple structures to match your preference

Cons

  • Harder to recover from; sleep and food matter more
  • Unevenly divided weeks in most structures
  • Missed sessions can leave gaps
  • Often unnecessary for beginners

Best for

  • Intermediate lifters wanting more weekly volume
  • People who enjoy gym time and recover well
  • Lifters preparing for physique goals with room for weak-point work

Think twice if…

  • Beginners — three or four days is usually enough
  • Anyone with an unpredictable schedule
  • People already short on sleep or recovery

Managing recovery on five days

Place your two rest days deliberately — after your hardest leg or deadlift day, and before the next heavy block. A Wed or Thu rest day splits the week well.

If you feel flat by day four or five, reduce sets on isolation exercises before cutting the main lifts. Persistent poor sleep, falling performance and loss of motivation are signs to drop to four days for a few weeks.

5-day workout split FAQ

Is a 5-day split good for beginners?

Usually not necessary. Beginners tend to progress well on three or four days and benefit from the extra recovery.

How do I split muscle groups over 5 days?

Either a PPL + upper/lower hybrid (most muscles twice weekly) or a body-part split (each muscle once). Pick based on whether you want frequency or focus.

Should I train 5 days in a row?

Avoid it if you can. Two rest days spread through the week make a 5-day plan far easier to sustain.
